A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HYPER research work. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables and figures are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material and distinguishing different evaluation settings.

before.justification: v1 reports original inductive link-prediction experiments, positional-encoding ablations and additional knowledge-graph evaluations in Section 5 and the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, argument-position corruption experiments and computational measurements.

M1.justification: The core encoders, message functions and training loss match after accounting for relocation to Appendix G.4. However, v1 G.2 initializes entities using a 'learned embedding' z_q, whereas v2 G.4 explicitly uses the relation encoder output h^(T)_{q|q}. The PDFs do not resolve whether this changes the computation or clarifies the earlier notation.

E1.justification: The 19 hypergraph benchmarks and 41 knowledge-graph evaluation datasets are retained. Section 5.5 adds corrupted argument-order scenarios across the 16 constructed datasets, introducing a distinct input condition. Larger HYPER pretraining mixtures use KG corpora already represented through ULTRA in v1.

E2.justification: v2 evaluates KG-ICL with four-, five- and six-layer encoders, whereas v1 only discussed this method. It also adds ULTRA pretrained on 4HG and 3KG+2HG, including a fine-tuned mixed-pretraining comparator in the hypergraph experiments. These substantially broaden the comparison beyond v1's KG-pretrained ULTRA variants.

E3.justification: The main KGFM evaluation switches from position edges plus separate relation nodes (†) to relation-and-position-specific edge types (‡); the original scheme remains an appendix comparison. v2 also adds matched pretraining controls, HYPER 4KG/50KG configurations, corruption of half the most frequent relation's hyperedges, and profiling at batch size 64. Existing benchmark splits and HYPER training schedules remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained positional-encoder ablation, v2 tests dependence on argument order through corruption (Section 5.5, Figure 6), sensitivity to reification choice (G.3, Table 11), and computational costs against ULTRA and HCNet (F.2, Table 10). These add substantial robustness, representation-choice and scalability analyses.

E5.justification: Section 5.1 broadens the stated scope of three-run averaging from end-to-end and fine-tuned experiments in v1 to 'the experiments' in v2. No increase in run count or new statistical test is documented. Zero-shot rows still lack standard deviations, leaving the practical extent of the broader statement unclear; added fine-tuned ULTRA rows follow the existing uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Existing HYPER scores and binary-KG results are retained, but v2 adds extensive pretraining-variant, KG-ICL, reification, corruption and runtime results. ULTRA(3KG) on JF-50 is 0.304 under the original † encoding and 0.437 under the new ‡ encoding, not a same-setting improvement. Original † MRRs for the 16 datasets survive in Table 11, while their Hits metrics and the original node-only † results are omitted. Figure 6 newly reports average MRR falling from 0.223 to 0.140 under corruption.

T1.justification: New Appendix C defines node-relation isomorphisms and invariants, proves HYPER's equivariance/invariance in Proposition C.1, and supplies an existence theorem and proof for positional-encoder injectivity, boundedness and Lipschitz continuity in Theorem C.2. These go substantially beyond v1's stated encoder requirements. The earlier complexity derivations are retained in F.1.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same novelty, arbitrary-arity generalization and hypergraph-performance contributions. The conclusion adds an explicit qualification that ULTRA generally performs better on standard knowledge-graph tasks, modestly narrowing the overall performance message.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations connecting positional corruption to lost semantic roles and reification behavior to hop distances, relation encoding and pretraining distributions. It interprets the measured computational overhead of the two encoders, acknowledges the ordinary-KG performance gap, and clarifies that unseen-relation percentages characterize end-to-end evaluation rather than zero-shot evaluation.

D1.justification: The code-access reference changes from an anonymous host to a named GitHub repository. v2 supplies the explicit sinusoidal encoding formula, KG-ICL depths and pretraining mixture, and model parameter counts and resource measurements. Most hardware disclosures, optimization hyperparameters and training schedules are retained; the repository's availability was not independently checked.

R1.justification: v2 adds RAILD (Gesese et al., 2022) and removes the standalone dataset references by Dettmers et al., Safavi and Koutra, and Toutanova and Chen. The principal positioning against binary-only KGFMs and hypergraph methods unable to handle unseen relations remains unchanged; the new capability table summarizes that positioning.

P1.justification: Most introductory and experimental prose remains recognizable. Section 4 is condensed by moving encoder equations into G.4, the complexity discussion is reorganized, and the former broader-impact paragraph becomes a main-text ethics statement. A reproducibility statement, local wording edits, and updated affiliations and publication headers accompany these changes.

P2.justification: v2 redraws Figure 4 for the new reification, redisplays the original beside it in Figure 7, and adds the corruption chart in Figure 6. It adds capability, scalability and comparison tables, expands and rearranges the main result tables, and splits the former detailed Table 15 into Tables 19–20. The conference template also changes typography and page layout.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses v1's unmatched-pretraining comparison with matched ULTRA controls, and adds useful reification, corruption, theoretical and computational analyses. However, new evidence contains unresolved reporting contradictions: Table 12 gives HYPER(3KG+2HG) average MRR 0.236, whereas its 16 Table 2 values average approximately 0.223; Table 21 reports ULTRA(4HG) WP-IND MRR 0.319 below Hits@1 0.330. These errors affect the added comparative evidence, preventing a reliable judgment of whether its benefits outweigh the loss of reporting reliability.
